name: Dana Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the recruitment team at a farm machinery manufacturer, the big one with the blue tractors, at their main plant outside town. There are five of us, and we fill around three hundred factory and office jobs a year: screening CVs, booking interviews, chasing references, sending offers. I've been team lead for five months, after my manager went on maternity leave and didn't come back. I'm still learning how to handle the hiring managers, who all think their job ad is the most urgent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly. I use it to sort CVs into a shortlist, draft the job ads and write the rejection emails, then I check everything. It's made my team about a third faster, and I'm not ashamed of that. I'm single, I rent a flat above the bakery on the high street, and I've got a couple of weeks of money saved, which my dad, who runs the hardware shop two doors down, tells me off about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that people oversold, and I'd keep using it. At work I'd say the companies that use it well still come out ahead. At church, honestly, nobody would ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, and maybe a bit relieved. My job's mostly people and judgement on top of the screening, so a modest tool just makes me faster. The real worry would be the same as now: low pay and almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep using the tools, and ask for a pay rise based on how much faster we are. I'd start saving properly, two hundred a month, because my dad's right. And I'd help Dad set up an online shop for the hardware store at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little uneasy about money. I like my job and I like the town. I'd just like a bit more in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help with the hardware shop online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the shop is struggling against the big DIY chain on the ring road. If Dad could sell online, the shop might last another ten years. And one day I might be the one running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to run it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. It's not glamorous, but it's ours, and people in town trust it. I'd rather own something small than be a number in something big.

I'd say firms that **use it well** still come out ahead.
think: I'd be fine, because my job is **people and judgement** on top of screening.
The real worry is **low pay** and almost nothing saved.
do: Ask for a **pay rise** based on the team's speed.
Save **two hundred a month**, as my dad keeps saying.
Help set up an **online shop** for my dad's hardware store.
feel: Mostly fine, a little **uneasy about money**.
S0.quote: I'd rather own something small than be a number in something big.
fieldNote: She sees AI as **her advantage**, not a threat, in a plateau.
Her **father's hardware shop** is a quiet long-term plan.
Her worry is **thin savings**, which her dad nags her about.

steps.text: Ask her manager for a pay rise using the faster hiring numbers
Set up a two-hundred-a-month savings transfer
Build an online shop for her dad's hardware store at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the market doing what markets do, and the people who adapt will be fine. At work I'd say let's be the team that does it first, not last. Online I'd share what we're learning, because it's good for my reputation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, screening and booking are on that card, so my team will shrink. Five might become two or three. But I'm the one who already does it with AI, so I think I'd be the one they keep, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month, I'd write up our AI process for the HR director and offer to roll it out to the other two plants. I'd make sure my team learns it too, so they've got a better chance. And I'd put more time into Dad's online shop, because that's a second income that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. I'd feel bad for the people who don't adapt. I'd also feel a bit proud that I saw it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sue, who's been booking interviews for fifteen years and hates the new system. Sue (the longest-serving coordinator on my team) is kind to every nervous candidate. I'd try to move Sue onto the face-to-face bits, but I can't promise anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said markets do what markets do. Should anyone help people like Sue?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, and employers, I think. The company should pay for training, not the government. Sue's family would rally round, and that's how it should be.

I'd want us to be **the team first**, not last.
think: Screening and booking are **on the card**, so my team will shrink.
I already use AI, so I'd likely be **the one kept**.
do: Offer to **roll out** our AI process to the other two plants.
Train my **team** so they've got a better chance.
Put more time into my dad's **online shop**.
feel: Uneasy but **a bit proud** she saw it coming.
S1.quote: Sue (the longest-serving coordinator on my team) is kind to every nervous candidate. I'd try to move Sue onto the face-to-face bits, but I can't promise anything.
fieldNote: She expects to **survive the cuts** because she's already the AI user.
She thinks **families and employers**, not the state, should catch people.
The **family shop** grows as a second income in her plans.

steps.text: Pitch the AI hiring process to the HR director for all three plants
Train her four coordinators on the AI shortlisting tools
Spend Saturdays growing her dad's online hardware shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock, but complaining won't stop it. At work I'd say let's make the most of the two years we've got. At church I'd say look after your families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job goes by 2028, AI or no AI skills. Recruitment is thinking work, all of it. But the hardware shop is hands-on, serving people and lifting stock, and that has until robots around 2031, maybe longer in a small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every bit of pay and experience out of the job for two years. I'd move in with my parents above the shop to save rent, and put the savings into the shop's stock and website. And I'd start working there properly, learning the stock and the trade customers, so I can take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had somewhere to go. Some of my friends would have nothing. I'd feel lucky and guilty at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shop survive when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not forever. But a robot doesn't know that Mr Patel (an old customer) on Elm Road always needs his paraffin in October. That kind of thing keeps a small shop alive longer than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is moving home a step back for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, at twenty-seven. But my family has always pulled together, and Mum would love it. I'd see it as investing in the shop, not giving up.

say: I'd say it's a **huge shock**, but complaining won't stop it.
I'd tell people at church to **look after families**.
think: Recruitment is all **thinking work**, so my job goes by 2028.
The **hardware shop** is hands-on and lasts until robots around 2031.
do: Squeeze **pay and experience** out of the job for two years.
Move in with my parents and put savings into **the shop**.
Start working at the shop to **take over** later.
feel: Lucky and **guilty** that friends have nothing.
S2.quote: A robot doesn't know that Mr Patel (an old customer) on Elm Road always needs his paraffin in October.
fieldNote: She uses the **robot delay** to plan a move into the family shop.
**Family** is her safety net, and she sees it as a strength.
She still expects her **job to go**, which keeps her anxious, not calm.

steps.text: Move in with her parents above the hardware shop

Work weekends in the shop learning stock and trade customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and people should use it instead of moaning. At work I'd encourage everyone to plan their next step. Online I'd share how I'm planning mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is almost ideal for me. I can build my HR experience for three years, then move to the shop properly around 2030, before AGI. And the shop's hands-on side has until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the AI rollout at work and ask for a proper title and pay for it. I'd take a short business course online in the evenings, to run the shop properly. And I'd start buying into the shop, a small share each year, so it's partly mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It feels like a plan I can actually see. Money's the only thing that could trip it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think about you buying in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say don't be silly, it's yours anyway one day. But I'd want to pay my way. It's how he raised me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the job offered you a promotion to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it, honestly. But a promotion in a recruitment job that ends in 2031 isn't much of a promotion. I'd take it for the money and keep the plan.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning** to use, not moan about.
I'd share **my own plan** online to encourage others.
think: Five years is **almost ideal**: build HR experience, then move to the shop.

Buy a **small share** of the shop each year.
feel: Uneasy but **mostly hopeful**, with money as the only risk.
S3.quote: A promotion in a recruitment job that ends in 2031 isn't much of a promotion. I'd take it for the money and keep the plan.
fieldNote: Five years fits her **two-stage plan** almost perfectly.
She'd **pay her way** into the family shop rather than wait to inherit.
Her outlook is **self-reliant**: plan, don't moan.

steps.text: Lead the AI hiring rollout and ask for a title and pay rise
Take an online small-business course in the evenings
Buy a small share of her dad's hardware shop each year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and anyone who's willing to work will find their way. At work I'd say keep learning and keep your options open. At church I'd probably say it's a time to be grateful we can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. I'd have years of AI experience, and the shop would be modern by then. I'd be thirty-seven, with a business that's partly mine and a skill that's rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going in recruitment and push for promotion, using AI every day. I'd build up the shop's online side slowly and maybe add a small trade-counter service. And I'd start putting some money into the shop and a pension, because there's finally time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. I've got a plan, a family and ten years. If I'm worried about anything, it's whether I'll meet someone and have kids before thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Does any of this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If anything, having the shop makes it easier, because it's flexible. My mum raised me behind the hardware shop counter, and I turned out fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friends who aren't planning. Some of them laugh at me for thinking this far ahead. I'd hate to watch them get caught out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, though less for me than for my friends. I'd have the shop, but two years is short for anyone. What would help is employers being honest early and paying for training, and banks lending to small family businesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. Everyone talks about big companies, but in a town like mine, a hardware shop that's been there forty years is what keeps people going. That's worth protecting.

headlineQuote: In a town like mine, a hardware shop that's been there forty years is what keeps people going. That's worth protecting.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old recruitment team lead** at a farm machinery manufacturer, managing five people.
She uses AI **every day** and expects to be kept when teams shrink.
Her father's **hardware shop** is her long-term plan and safety net.
She's **self-reliant**, trusting family and employers over government.
She's **anxious** at most in the fast scenario, and calm with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for friends who aren't planning ahead.
whatWouldHelp: Employers being **honest early** and paying for training.
